parsed.why: No criminalisation, no facilities or border restrictions; but documented police extortion of trans people, impunity warnings from the regional commission, protests over killings, and state-level recognition gaps. Strong paper rights with weak, uneven enforcement.

State-imposed universal exposure: passport markers reversed, X barred, document discrepancy a refusal/fraud ground, trans athletes banned, bathroom bans enforced by arrest, birth-sex custody with reported abuse, allied government advisories to trans travellers.

Criminalised same-sex conduct reachable indirectly, no gender recognition, police/prosecutors documented refusing to investigate anti-LGBTQ crimes, hostile society (15% local acceptance). Thin data resolved toward the structural risk. No organised trans-specific state targeting.

No criminalisation, constitutional and Supreme Court recognition, visible Pride and civil society; offset by no workable document-change procedure, documented discrimination and physical/sexual harassment of visibly trans people in provincial public life, and rising political hostility.

No criminalisation, decriminalised since 1992, rule-of-law state with courts reopening hate-crime prosecutions after regional court ruling; gaps in hate-crime enforcement and no gender-identity protections, but no trans-specific police, facilities or border exposure documented.
